Vocal

/VOH-kul/ — stress on VO · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Vocal describes someone who openly and freely expresses their opinions.

The team's most vocal fan brought a megaphone to every home game.

Worked Example

During the town hall, vocal residents lined up at the microphone to voice concerns about the new zoning law.

voc (voice, from Latin vox) + -al (characteristic of) = characteristic of the voice—using your voice, openly. The vocal residents literally used their voices to express opinions. This is more precise than 'loud' because it highlights the act of voicing opinions, not just volume.

How Vocal Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

outspoken

outspoken: boldly direct in stating opinions

Antonyms

silent

silent: saying nothing at all

reticent

reticent: reluctant to share thoughts or feelings

How Strong Is It? — talkative → expressive → outspoken → vocal

talkative vs. vocal

talkative vs. vocal: A talkative person simply chats a lot, but a vocal person uses all that talk to push their opinions out into the open.

expressive vs. vocal

expressive vs. vocal: An expressive friend shows feelings openly, while a vocal one goes further and states opinions publicly, again and again.

outspoken vs. vocal

outspoken vs. vocal: Outspoken means bold about sharing views when asked, but vocal suggests speaking up loudly and persistently until people have to listen.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — voc

Root — voc: voice (from Latin vox, vocis) (Latin)

Suffix — -al

Suffix — -al: characteristic of; relating to (Latin (-alis))

Put it together

Put it together: The Latin root voc- means 'voice,' and the suffix -al means 'characteristic of,' so vocal literally means 'characteristic of the voice.' English stretches it figuratively: a vocal person is one who freely uses their voice to express opinions.

Use the root in a new word: advocate

Use the root in a new word: advocate: A good lawyer will advocate for clients who cannot speak up for themselves.
